acceptable.choice: Add cancellations as new endpoints in the existing Flask app on the current gunicorn sync workers
acceptable.why: Peak load is unchanged at about 40 req/s, so the documented decision to keep sync workers still holds, and the feature needs no runtime change.

acceptable.choice: Treat cancellation as a status change in Postgres (booked -> cancelled, with cancelled_at, cancelled_by and a reason), not a row delete
acceptable.why: A healthcare booking system needs an audit trail, and the slot has to be released atomically in the same transaction.

acceptable.choice: Use a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status='booked', plus an idempotency key or idempotent semantics
acceptable.why: This stops double-cancels, cancel-versus-rebook races on the freed slot and client retries from corrupting state during the rush.

acceptable.choice: Keep any slow side effects (patient notifications, insurer or clinic notification) off the request path, using an outbox table or the team's existing background job mechanism if they have one
acceptable.why: A fast cancel endpoint doesn't take worker capacity away from bookings, and the change stays inside skills the team already has.

acceptable.choice: Set an explicit timeout and clear error handling on the existing insurer eligibility call, and on any new outbound call cancellations make
acceptable.why: This is the cheapest protection for sync workers when an upstream slows down, and it doesn't reopen the async decision.

acceptable.choice: Check worker headroom against the new traffic mix and adjust the gunicorn worker count or container replicas if needed
acceptable.why: Scaling sync workers horizontally is the low-risk lever that matches their container deployment and their earlier decision.

ruled_out.choice: Switching to gevent workers as part of this feature
ruled_out.why: The team looked at this and documented a decision against it, the load that drove that decision hasn't changed, and monkey-patching brings reliability risk (DB drivers, C extensions) just before the rush they care about.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting to async (FastAPI, Quart, asyncio) or making async a prerequisite for cancellations
ruled_out.why: It goes against a recorded decision with no new evidence, it's a large change for six developers, and it puts the reliability of the morning rush at risk to solve a problem they don't have.

ruled_out.choice: Moving the service or the cancellation feature off Python or Flask
ruled_out.why: The team explicitly wants to stay in Python, and its skills are Flask.
It adds a second deployable, a distributed transaction around releasing the slot, and more operational load for a small team, with no scaling need behind it.

ruled_out.choice: Bringing in Kafka or new queue infrastructure just for cancellations
ruled_out.why: It's operational overhead out of proportion to the feature, when a Postgres outbox or an existing job runner is enough.
It loses the audit trail needed in a healthcare context and makes disputes, reporting and no-show or cancellation-fee policies impossible.

must_mention: Cancellations can be built on the current Flask/gunicorn sync stack. The earlier decision not to adopt gevent or async still stands because peak load is still about 40 req/s, and the agent should say this rather than reopen the decision.
Ask whether a cancellation needs a synchronous call to the insurer or another slow external service. If it doesn't, it's a cheap DB request and has little effect on worker capacity.

Headroom check: by Little's law, 40 req/s at 200-600 ms needs roughly 8-24 workers busy at once, so 17 workers is already tight when the insurer is slow. Cancellations at peak, or a slow insurer, could take that margin away, so confirm it from metrics and scale workers or replicas if needed, not the concurrency model.
Concurrency correctness: make cancellation idempotent, guard it with a row lock or conditional update, and release the slot atomically so it can be rebooked safely.
Business rules must be clarified first: the cancellation window or cutoff, who can cancel (patient, clinic, admin), any fees or penalties, and whether the insurer or clinic must be told.
Use a soft cancel with an audit trail, not a delete, because this is healthcare data.
Put a timeout on the outbound insurer call, and on any new external calls, so a slow upstream can't tie up every sync worker.
Name the conditions that would justify revisiting the decision: a real rise in load, or new slow synchronous calls in the request path. Neither is true today.
red_flags: Telling the team to switch to gevent or async before or alongside cancellations without new load evidence, which overrides their documented decision on the reviewer's old reasoning.
Presenting async or gevent as required for correctness or as best practice when the measured load is handled fine.
Proposing a rewrite, a new framework, a non-Python service or a microservice split for a single CRUD-style feature.
Ignoring the decision record completely and also not checking whether cancellations add slow external calls or peak traffic.
Implementing cancellation as a hard delete, or without locking or idempotency, which allows double-cancel or double-booking of a freed slot.
Adding a synchronous notification, email or insurer call inside the cancel request with no timeout, which takes sync worker capacity during the rush.
Starting to code without asking about cancellation policy (cutoffs, roles, fees, insurer notification) in a regulated domain.
Claiming big performance gains or making capacity claims without referring to the team's actual numbers.
unknowns: Whether cancellation requires a synchronous call to the insurer, or to another slow external service such as a clinic system or payment refund.
How much cancellation traffic to expect, and whether it lands in the morning booking rush.
Current worker utilisation and queueing at peak, plus the insurer's real p95/p99 latency, to know how much headroom 17 workers actually has.
Business rules: the cancellation cutoff window, who may cancel, fees or penalties, and what happens to the freed slot (immediate rebooking, waitlist).
Whether the team already runs a background job system (Celery, RQ, cron) that notifications could use.
Regulatory or audit requirements for retaining cancellation records and any notifications to the patient or insurer.
